references.text: Joseph assures his brothers that it was God's plan to send him ahead of them to preserve life. This is the direct parallel to Gen 50:20, where Joseph again confirms that his brothers' evil actions served God's good purpose.
The psalm describes how God sent Joseph ahead—he was sold as a slave—as part of God's plan to preserve the people, which directly mirrors Joseph's realization in Gen 50:20.

God uses Assyria as an instrument of His judgment, even though Assyria itself has evil intentions. This illustrates the same principle found in Gen 50:20: humans plan evil, but God uses it to fulfill His purpose.
Paul states that all things work together for good for those who love God, a principle that directly reflects Joseph's recognition that God turned his brothers' evil into something good.

The believers recognize that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel only carried out what God's hand and plan had foreordained, showing how God uses human evil actions to fulfill His good purposes—the same principle as in Gen 50:20.

Peter preaches that Jesus was handed over according to God's set plan and foreknowledge, but that God raised Him up. This shows that human evil actions (the crucifixion) served God's plan of salvation.
A direct narrative parallel confirming Joseph's theological interpretation of his brothers' betrayal as part of God's rescue plan.
A thematic parallel concerning God's sovereign hand giving enemies into one's power, and the human choice to let God repay rather than take revenge oneself.
Direct textual and narrative connection; the verses are part of the same speech where Joseph states God's purpose in sending him to Egypt.
